NOTICE 341; AND (2) OTHER                                )

SOUTHWESTERN PUBLIC SERVICE COMPANY’S RESPONSE IN OPPOSITION TO
              STAFF’S MOTION FOR ORAL ARGUMENT

       Southwestern Public Service Company (“SPS”) submits this Response in Opposition to the

Commission Utility Division Staff’s (“Staff”) Motion for Oral Argument (“Motion”), pursuant to

the Commission’s Order Granting Leave to File Responses to Exceptions and Order Requiring

Response to Staff’s Motion for Oral Argument, issued on November 5, 2026 (“November 5

Order”). Staff identifies no reason for the Commission to grant oral argument on the issues

identified in the Motion, which are predominantly factual issues that Staff litigated and lost. Oral

argument is unnecessary in these circumstances, and the Motion should be denied.

       I.      INTRODUCTION

       The Commission’s procedural rules do not entitle Staff to oral argument on exceptions to

a certification of stipulation. Although the Commission may allow oral argument in its discretion,

Staff identifies no reason to exercise that discretion here. As discussed below, none of the cases

Staff cites establish that oral argument would assist the Commission in reviewing the Certification

of Stipulation (“Certification”) in this instance.




                                                     1
        Oral argument on factual disputes that the hearing examiners considered and rejected is

unnecessary and will duplicate much of the evidence already presented and in the record. Staff had

ample opportunity to make its case; propounded voluminous written discovery for months;

presented multiple rounds of testimony; cross-examined witnesses during a four-day hearing; filed

two rounds of post-hearing briefs; and submitted exceptions to the Certification. In the 156-page

Certification, the Hearing Examiners thoroughly considered and rejected the same arguments Staff

now seeks to present via oral argument. Moreover, the Commission’s November 5 Order

authorizes responses to Staff's Exceptions, providing yet another opportunity for the parties to

address those issues in writing. Accordingly, given the extensive briefing and discovery in this

case, Staff’s request for oral argument is unfounded and should be denied.

       Staff also fails to explain how oral argument is procedurally appropriate. Staff’s

disagreement with the Certification is not a reason to re-argue the case. In essence, Staff’s Motion

amounts to a motion for reconsideration of the Certification. It seeks another opportunity to argue

issues already litigated and decided without identifying new evidence or an unsettled question of

law.

       The Motion also presents a practical timing concern given that the suspension period ends

on November 30, 2026. Scheduling oral argument would complicate an already compressed

schedule without providing a corresponding benefit. For these reasons, the Commission should

deny the Motion.




                                                 2
         II.      ARGUMENT

              1. Neither the Commission’s rules nor Staff’s cited authorities establish a need
                 for oral argument on the Certification.

        Although the Commission may allow oral argument on motions in its discretion, 1 neither

this rule nor the rule governing exceptions to certifications of stipulation 2 entitles Staff to oral

argument. Staff’s reliance on Section 62-19-20(C) is misplaced. That provision states that at least

one Commissioner must attend oral argument upon a party’s request when a hearing examiner has

been appointed. In other words, it governs a Commissioner’s attendance at oral argument before a

hearing examiner, not whether the Commission should grant oral argument in the first place. The

question is whether oral argument would assist the Commission in resolving the issues presented

here. Staff has not shown that it would. 3

        The Commission has previously denied oral argument on exceptions to a hearing

examiner’s recommended decision when the oral argument would merely duplicate earlier

argument. In In re TerraCom, Inc., Case No. 11-00135-UT, the Commission found that the

arguments raised in the exceptions were “substantially the same as those that were raised to the

hearing examiner,” rejected the exceptions, and denied a motion for oral argument. 4 Likewise, in

In re Mesilla Park Service, LLC d/b/a Yellowbird Solar, Case No. 23-00074-UT, the Commission

resolved disputed questions concerning the Community Solar Act without oral argument. 5 These

orders illustrate that the Commission routinely resolves contested issues on the written record

without granting oral argument.


        1
         See 1.2.2.37(D) NMAC.
        2
         See 1.2.2.20(B)(5)(b) NMAC.
       3
         See Case No. 23-00119-UT, Final Order, Ex. B, 1.2.2.20(C)(6)(b) NMAC (Aug. 27, 2026).
       4
         Case No. 11-00135-UT, Final Order ¶ 7, Ordering ¶¶ D–E (May 15, 2013).
       5
         Case No. 23-00074-UT, Order Partially Granting Requests for Clarification and Denying Motion for Oral
Argument and Expedited Responses ¶¶ 19–21, Ordering ¶ A (Mar. 22, 2023)


                                                      3
        Although Staff characterizes its proposed argument here as “legal rather than factual,” 6 the

issue set forth in the Motion involves disputed facts concerning linkage data and jurisdictional

allocation. Invoking the legal standard of “fair, just, and reasonable” rates does not explain why

oral argument would assist the Commission in resolving these factual disputes.

       Additionally, the three Commission orders Staff cites do not weigh in favor of holding oral

argument. Each involved a distinct legal question or unique procedural circumstance. In Case No.

15-00261-UT, the Commission allowed oral argument after the New Mexico Supreme Court

vacated a final rate order on the ground that the Commission had violated PNM’s constitutional

right to due process. The Supreme Court remanded the case, leaving the Commission to determine

how to proceed consistently with the Court’s mandate. 7 Here, by contrast, Staff identifies no

comparable due-process violation, appellate mandate, or unresolved question concerning the scope

of a remand. It simply disagrees with the Hearing Examiners.

       Similarly, in Case No. 15-00127-UT, the Commission permitted oral argument on

interlocutory appeals arising from the Hearing Examiner’s rulings on motions to dismiss. Those

appeals raised threshold legal questions concerning El Paso Electric Company’s proposed

distributed-generation rate, many being addressed for the first time. 8 The Commission identified

six specific questions of statutory and regulatory interpretation for argument. Id. ¶ 3. In this case,

Staff disputes how the Hearing Examiners applied settled ratemaking requirements to the evidence.

The Motion identifies no novel statutory or regulatory question for which oral argument would

assist the Commission.




       6
         Motion ¶ 2,
       7
         Case No. 15-00261-UT, Order on Remand ¶¶ 1–3 (Jan. 8, 2020)
       8
         Case No. 15-00127-UT, Order Granting Motions for Oral Argument ¶ 2 (Sept. 30, 2015).


                                                     4
        Finally, Case No. 24-00269-UT involved oral argument the Hearing Examiners themselves

requested at the close of the evidentiary hearing. They sought the parties’ views on the legal

implications of a recently issued Commission order concerning avoided-emissions benefits. 9 That

is a far cry from Staff’s request for another round of argument after the Hearing Examiners issued

an exhaustive Certification rejecting Staff’s arguments.

       Staff thoroughly presented its case and the Hearing Examiners considered and rejected the

arguments Staff now seeks to present orally. Staff’s disagreement with the Certification neither

necessitates nor warrants further argument and would not further assist the Commission in

deciding its Exceptions. Another round of argument would duplicate the extensive evidentiary

record and written submissions already before the Commission.

             2. Relitigating factual disputes through oral argument would not assist the
                Commission.

       Although the Motion states that Staff seeks oral argument to resolve “contested legal

issues” related to the Certification, the Motion primarily identifies factual disputes that Staff

litigated unsuccessfully and has renewed in its Exceptions. Staff does not explain why those

disputes require oral argument rather than resolution on the existing record.

       The parties extensively litigated whether SPS should have to adjust its forecasted New

Mexico jurisdictional allocators to account for Texas’s historical ratemaking. The Hearing

Examiners unequivocally rejected Staff's position, holding that “Texas’s use of historical

allocation factors is not a reason to prohibit SPS from using forecasted jurisdictional allocation

factors in a FTY rate case filing in New Mexico.” 10 They further concluded that differences

between the two states’ ratemaking methods do not by themselves establish that SPS’s New



       9
           Case No. 24-00269-UT, Order on Prehearing Matters ¶ 3 (May 21, 2025).
       10
           Certification ¶ 75.


                                                      5
 Mexico rates are unreasonable. 11 Staff’s Motion fails to identify a reason why oral argument would

assist the Commission in reviewing that determination.

       Likewise, SPS supported its future test year and linkage data through testimony and

exhibits. Staff challenged that evidence at hearing and in post-hearing briefing. The Hearing

Examiners thoroughly considered Staff's arguments and rejected them. The Certification found

that SPS complied with the Future Test Year Rule’s requirements for updating data. 12 Staff repeats

this objection in its Exceptions, 13 but does not identify any legal reason that oral argument would

add to this analysis.

       Staff also presents unsubstantiated allegations as established facts. For example, the

Motion asserts that differences between Texas and New Mexico test periods “will cause

overcollection” from New Mexico customers when the Hearing Examiners never adopted that

finding. As the Hearing Examiners recognized, because of differences between the two states, SPS

could overcollect or undercollect its systemwide revenue requirement at times without rendering

New Mexico rates unreasonable. 14 Staff presents as established fact what the Hearing Examiners–

and Staff itself–recognized as only a possibility.

       At bottom, Staff’s Motion combines two distinct, thoroughly litigated factual issues into a

single, argumentative question and then claims the question is a legal one that warrants oral

argument . Neither the Commission’s rules nor the orders Staff cites demonstrate that oral

argument would assist the Commission in evaluating the issues raised by the Motion . That Staff

disagrees with the Certification does not justify another round of argument, particularly because




       11
          Id. ¶¶ 72–74.
       12
          Id. ¶¶ 95–134; 17.1.3 NMAC.
       13
          Staff’s Exceptions Nos. 3–5.
       14
          Certification ¶ 74.


                                                     6
 the Commission already authorized additional briefing on Staff's Exceptions. Thus, the

Commission should deny Staff’s Motion.

       III.    CONCLUSION

       Staff identifies no issue for which oral argument would materially assist the Commission's

review in this proceeding. Instead, the Motion repackages factual disputes the parties have already

litigated and that Staff has renewed in its Exceptions. The Commission can resolve those disputes

on the existing record without further argument or delay. For the foregoing reasons, SPS

respectfully requests that the Commission deny Staff’s Motion for Oral Argument.

                                                 Respectfully submitted,
